client: I lost my dog last month, and honestly, things just haven't felt the same since. I used to love going for morning walks or just watching TV in the evenings, but now those things feel kind of hollow and pointless without him there. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because it's not like anything can bring him back.
therapist: Losing a companion like that leaves such a deep, quiet kind of ache — the absence shows up in all those small, everyday moments you shared together, and that hollow feeling makes complete sense. I hear some doubt in your voice about whether talking will help, and that's a really honest thing to name; grief can make even reaching out feel pointless. I'm curious — even if nothing can bring him back, what do you think it might feel like to have a space where his memory and what he meant to you could just be... acknowledged?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess there's something a little comforting about the idea of that, like maybe just saying his name out loud and talking about what he was like without someone trying to fix it or move me along. But I also worry that talking about him too much will just make it worse, like I'll spiral into it and not be able to get back out. It's hard to know if sitting with it is healing or just... reopening something that's barely starting to close.
therapist: That fear of spiraling is such a common and understandable one — like if you open the door too wide, you won't be able to close it again. What's worth noticing, though, is that grief tends to be more like waves than a spiral; visiting the memory of him doesn't necessarily pull you under, it can actually help your nervous system learn that you can hold the pain *and* come back up. I wonder — what would it feel like to just start small, like telling me one thing about who he was?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: His name was Biscuit, and he was this scruffy little terrier mix who always somehow knew when I was having a bad day and would just plant himself right on my lap. Saying that just now actually didn't feel as terrible as I expected, which is a little surprising. But I'm not sure I fully buy the wave thing yet, because right now it just feels like one long wave that never really breaks.
therapist: Biscuit sounds like he had a real gift for showing up for you in exactly the right way — that kind of quiet, intuitive presence is so rare and so deeply missed. It's meaningful that saying his name felt a little more okay than you feared; that's not a small thing, even if it doesn't feel like proof of anything yet. And I hear you on the long wave — maybe right now we're not looking for it to break, just noticing that you're still here, still riding it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That framing of just "still riding it" actually sits better with me than the idea of getting over it or healing, because getting over it feels like a betrayal somehow, like I'd be leaving him behind. But I still feel this guilt when I have a moment where I'm not thinking about him, like I'm already forgetting, and then I feel terrible about it. I don't know if that makes any sense or if it's just me being irrational.
therapist: What you're describing makes complete sense — that guilt is actually a sign of how much you loved him, not a sign that you're forgetting. I notice as you're saying this, there's something in your voice that sounds quieter, almost a little deflated, like the words are carrying more weight than they might appear to on the surface — I wonder if underneath the guilt there's also something that feels like exhaustion, like it's tiring to hold all of this so carefully? In CBT we'd gently challenge the idea that a moment of relief or distraction is a betrayal — those moments don't erase Biscuit, they're actually how you survive loving someone you've lost.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, exhausted is actually exactly the right word, because it does feel like a full-time job just managing how I'm supposed to feel about all of this. I hear what you're saying about those moments of relief not being a betrayal, and part of me wants to believe that, but another part of me thinks that's just something people say to make grief feel more manageable. Like, how do I actually get from knowing that intellectually to feeling it, because right now the guilt still hits just as hard even when I remind myself of that?
therapist: That gap between knowing something and *feeling* it is one of the most frustrating parts of grief — your mind can hold the logic while your nervous system is still running on a completely different timeline. What's interesting is that you're speaking quite quickly right now, like there's a lot pressing to get out, but your voice also sounds quite soft and a little worn — which makes me think part of you already knows this truth about relief not being betrayal, and is maybe just tired of having to keep arguing for it against the guilt. The shift tends to happen less through convincing yourself and more through collecting small moments of evidence — each time you have a breath of relief and Biscuit is still just as real and loved afterward, your nervous system slowly starts to trust that.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: That idea of collecting small moments of evidence is interesting, but I'm not sure how I'd even notice them in the moment when the guilt tends to hit so fast and loud that it drowns everything else out. Like, it's not that I don't want to trust that he's still real to me even when I'm not actively grieving, it's that the guilt doesn't really give me a chance to pause and reflect before it's already made me feel terrible. I guess I'm wondering if there's something more concrete I could actually do in those moments, because just observing them feels a bit passive for how overwhelming it gets.
therapist: You're asking exactly the right question — noticing isn't enough when the guilt moves faster than your thoughts, so having something concrete to *do* gives you a way to interrupt that automatic cycle before it lands. One thing that can help in CBT is a simple grounding phrase you prepare in advance — something like "I loved him then, I love him now" — so that when the guilt hits, you're not trying to construct a counter-argument from scratch but reaching for something already true and already yours. Would it feel worth trying to find a few words like that, something that feels genuinely like *you*, that you could have ready for those fast moments?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I like the idea in theory, but I worry that in the moment it'll just feel like a hollow thing I'm saying to myself, like a mantra that doesn't really mean anything because the guilt is too loud to hear it. I think the phrase you suggested is actually pretty close to something I could mean, but I'd want it to feel less like a coping trick and more like something true about me and Biscuit specifically. Maybe something more like "he knew I loved him, and that doesn't go away" — because one of the things I keep coming back to is whether he knew, and I think deep down I believe he did.
therapist: "He knew I loved him, and that doesn't go away" — that's not a coping trick, that's just the truth, and you arrived at it yourself, which means it will actually hold weight when you need it. There's something really significant in the fact that you *do* believe he knew, even through the grief — that belief is yours, it's real, and the guilt can't actually take it away even when it's loud. I'd gently encourage you to let that phrase belong to you and Biscuit now, not as something to silence the guilt, but as a true thing you can stand on while the guilt does what it does.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Hearing it framed that way, as something to stand on rather than something to fight the guilt with, actually makes it feel less fragile somehow. I think I've been approaching all of this like I need to win an argument against my own feelings, and that's exhausting in a way I hadn't quite named before. I'm still not sure how the next hard moment will go, but I think I'll try to hold onto that phrase and see if it feels different when it's coming from me rather than just something I'm supposed to say.
therapist: That shift you just named — from fighting your feelings to having something to stand on — is actually a meaningful one, and the fact that you found the words for it yourself says a lot about the work you're doing here. Your voice sounds a little stretched, like you're carrying something carefully, which makes sense given how much you've been holding today. Whatever the next hard moment looks like, you don't have to have it figured out in advance — you just have that one true thing, and that's enough to start with.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think this is the first time in a while that I've talked about Biscuit without feeling worse afterward, which is strange and a little hard to trust, like I'm waiting for the guilt to catch up with me. I'm still a bit skeptical that one phrase is going to hold up against the really bad moments, like the evenings when the couch feels especially empty. But I think I came in here not believing talking would help at all, and something did shift a little, so maybe that's worth sitting with.
therapist: What you just said is worth sitting with — you came in doubting this would help at all, and something shifted anyway, and that's not nothing, that's actually evidence. I notice your voice sounds quite soft and a little quieter than your words, like part of you is holding this realization gently, almost carefully, as if it might slip away — and I think that carefulness makes sense when something feels fragile and new. The skepticism about the hard evenings is fair and honest, but you don't have to trust it fully yet; you just found out today that talking about Biscuit can feel different than you expected, and that's a real thing that happened.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think that's fair, and I don't want to talk myself out of it before I've even left the room, which is something I have a tendency to do. It's just that the evenings are when it really hits, and I guess I'm already bracing for tonight without even meaning to. Maybe I'll try to just notice if the phrase helps at all, and not decide ahead of time whether it will or won't work.
therapist: That last thing you said — "not deciding ahead of time whether it will or won't work" — is actually a really healthy instinct, and it's worth noticing that you caught yourself bracing and named it, which is itself a kind of pause before the guilt or dread takes over. Tonight might be hard, and that's okay; you're not going in empty-handed anymore. You have something true to stand on, and you have the knowledge that you got through today differently than you expected — that counts for something when the couch feels quiet.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
